CPP pension sharing between spouses: the months-together formula, who gains and when it can cost tax

A worked guide to Canada Pension Plan pension sharing (assignment): how Service Canada’s formula uses months living together in the joint contributory period, why both pensions are shared, what changes when one spouse never contributed, why sharing can raise a couple’s tax, and what happens when it ends. Five charts and an editable model.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 8 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

The central idea

Pension sharing moves real CPP payments between spouses. Each base pension is shareable in the ratio of months lived together to months in the joint contributory period, half of each shareable amount goes to the other spouse, and only the difference changes hands. The couple’s combined CPP never changes; the tax result depends on who has the higher marginal rate, and the formula offers no percentage to choose.

01

Sharing moves money, not just taxable income

CPP pension sharing—the Act calls it an assignment of a retirement pension—lets spouses or common-law partners who live together redistribute the part of their CPP retirement pensions earned while they were together. Unlike the T1032 pension income splitting election, which only reallocates income between two tax returns, sharing changes the monthly payments each person receives from Service Canada. Each spouse then reports their own adjusted CPP on their return.

Three features shape the planning. First, if both spouses have CPP pensions, both are shared; you cannot share only the larger one. Second, the couple’s combined CPP does not change—Service Canada states this directly—so any benefit comes from tax and income-tested benefits, not from more pension. Third, sharing begins the month after Service Canada approves the application and cannot be backdated, so the decision has a cost of delay when it is favourable.

The CPP post-retirement benefit (PRB) earned by working after the pension starts is not included in sharing. QPP pensions follow Retraite Québec’s rules. CPP and QPP retirement pensions also cannot be split through Form T1032; the related pension-splitting guide covers that separate election.

02

Who can apply

Service Canada requires that you live with your legal spouse or common-law partner and that you, your partner or both receive (or have applied for) a CPP retirement pension. A common-law partner under the CPP is someone who has lived with you in a conjugal relationship for at least one year, and spouses who are voluntarily separated when they apply cannot be approved. Either spouse can apply, online through My Service Canada Account or on paper with form ISP1002, and both social insurance numbers go on every document.

Section 65.1 of the Canada Pension Plan Act sets out two situations. If both spouses are contributors, both must be receiving a retirement pension, and the assignment applies to both. If only one ever contributed to the CPP or a provincial plan, the non-contributor must be at least 60 and only the contributor’s pension is shared. A written agreement or court order generally does not bind the Minister; the Act’s narrow exception is a post-4 June 1986 agreement that refers to the Act and expresses an intention that no assignment be made, where provincial law permits it.

03

The formula: months together ÷ months in the joint contributory period

Section 65.1(9) assigns, from each pension, 50% of the pension multiplied by the ratio of months of cohabitation to months in the joint contributory period. The joint contributory period starts in January 1966 or the month the older spouse turns 18, whichever is later, and ends when the later of the two individual contributory periods ends—usually when the second spouse’s pension starts. If only one spouse is a contributor, it ends at the earlier of the month the non-contributor turns 70 and the month of approval. Some excluded months, such as months of CPP disability, can be removed. Your Statement of Contributions shows the details Service Canada will use.

The three CPP components and their sharing periods (CPP Act s. 65.1(8)–(9))
ComponentPeriod used in the ratio startsPractical effect
Base pensionJanuary 1966 or the older spouse’s 18th birthdayLong period; couples who met later share a smaller fraction
First additional (enhancement)1 January 2019A couple together since 2019 shares it at the full 50%
Second additional (enhancement)1 January 2024Same, from 2024

Because each spouse gives half of their shareable amount and receives half of the other’s, the net transfer is half of the difference between the two shareable amounts. If both spouses lived together for the whole period, the result is two equal pensions. The model reproduces the base and enhancement pieces separately; it does not calculate the pieces themselves, which come from your contribution record.

04

Worked example: CAD 1,250 and CAD 440 become CAD 939.79 and CAD 750.21

Hypothetical couple, both 65 or older in 2026. Pat receives CAD 1,250 a month of CPP (CAD 1,100 base and CAD 150 enhancement); Lee receives CAD 440 (CAD 400 base and CAD 40 enhancement). For scale, the maximum for a new CPP retirement pension at 65 starting in January 2026 is CAD 1,507.65 a month. The joint contributory period runs 576 months—from the older spouse’s 18th birthday to the month the second pension started 48 years later—and they lived together for 420 of those months, all of them since 2019.

The base ratio is 420 ÷ 576 = 72.92%. Pat’s shareable amount is 72.92% × 1,100 + 150 = CAD 952.08; Lee’s is 72.92% × 400 + 40 = CAD 331.67. Half the difference, CAD 310.21 a month, moves from Pat to Lee: Pat now receives CAD 939.79 and Lee CAD 750.21, still CAD 1,690 together. Over 12 months that moves CAD 3,722.50 of taxable income.

With CAD 45,000 of other income for Pat (including CAD 9,150 of OAS and CAD 30,000 of eligible pension) and CAD 12,000 for Lee (all but CAD 2,850 of it OAS), Pat’s net income falls from CAD 60,000 to CAD 56,277.50. That removes CAD 1,477 from the 20.5% bracket and CAD 2,245.50 at 14%, and restores CAD 558.38 of age amount, for an illustrative federal saving of CAD 695.33. Lee’s tax stays at zero: Lee’s 2026 basic personal and age amounts (CAD 25,660 at 14%) still exceed the bracket tax on CAD 21,002.50. Provincial tax would add to the effect and is not modelled.

05

How months together, a late marriage or a non-contributing spouse change the result

The months-together chart shows the base part scaling in a straight line. With the default pensions, a couple who lived together for the full 576 months would end with equal pensions of CAD 845 each (a CAD 405 transfer); a couple who married after both pensions had started would have no base months together, but if they were together for the enhancement periods the enhancement parts still produce a CAD 55 transfer. For a recently formed couple, the enhancement share you enter matters more than it first appears, because those periods start only in 2019 and 2024.

When one spouse never contributed, only the contributor’s pension is shared and the period runs to the non-contributor’s 70th birthday month or approval, whichever is earlier. In a variant with Lee as a non-contributor, a 624-month period and 480 months together, 76.92% of Pat’s base plus the full enhancement is shareable, and CAD 498.08 a month moves to Lee. Sharing ends if the non-contributor later starts contributing.

06

When sharing raises tax—and why there is no dial

Pension sharing helps only when it moves income from the spouse with the higher marginal cost to the one with the lower cost. The formula is mechanical: there is no percentage to choose, and both pensions move. Reverse the default pensions so that Lee, the spouse with less other income, has the larger CPP, and sharing moves CAD 310.21 a month toward Pat. Pat pays about 16.1% on each extra dollar (14% plus the age-amount reduction), while Lee saves only the CAD 187.60 of tax Lee was paying; the couple pays an illustrative CAD 411.72 more federal tax. In that household the right decision is not to apply.

At the other end, sharing can reduce OAS recovery tax. With Pat’s other income raised to CAD 100,000 (net income CAD 115,000 before sharing), moving CAD 3,722.50 saves 20.5% bracket tax and 15% OAS recovery on every dollar: an illustrative CAD 1,321.49 a year. Sharing can be combined with a T1032 election for other pension income in the same year; the order of effects matters and should be tested on actual returns.

Income-tested benefits react too. The Guaranteed Income Supplement, provincial seniors’ credits and the GST/HST credit use net income, and sharing changes each spouse’s net income even though household income is unchanged. The model covers federal income tax and OAS recovery only.

07

When sharing stops, the pensions revert

Under section 65.1(11) and Service Canada’s page, sharing ends at the earliest of: the month after Service Canada approves a joint cancellation request (form ISP1014); the month of a divorce or nullity judgment; the month either spouse dies; the 12th month after the couple begin living separate and apart (for CPP and QPP pensions, the earlier of that and a legal separation); and, for a non-contributor, the month they begin contributing. Either spouse may later ask in writing for an ended assignment to be reinstated.

When sharing ends, each pension returns to what it would have been without sharing. In the worked example, Lee’s payment would drop from CAD 750.21 back to CAD 440 and Pat’s would rise to CAD 1,250. A budget that treats the shared amount as permanent personal income can be exposed in a separation; on a death, the CPP survivor’s pension follows separate rules and is not modelled here. Pension sharing is also different from a division of CPP credits after separation, which redistributes contribution records rather than payments.

08

Planning checklist and model limits

  • Get the record first. Download the Statement of Contributions for both spouses; the base and enhancement amounts and the joint contributory period come from it.
  • Test the direction. Sharing helps only when net money moves to the lower-taxed spouse. If the lower-income spouse has the larger CPP, it can cost tax.
  • Apply promptly if it helps. Sharing starts the month after approval and is not retroactive.
  • Coordinate with T1032 and benefits. Check the pension-splitting election, GIS, provincial credits and OAS recovery together.
  • Plan for reversal. Divorce, a 12-month separation or a death ends sharing; the household budget should survive the original pension amounts.

The model applies the section 65.1(9) ratio with one combined enhancement share, assumes 12 months of sharing in 2026, ignores the PRB, excluded months and QPP, and uses only federal tax and OAS recovery with both spouses 65 or older. It is an explanation of the mechanics, not a Service Canada calculation or tax advice.
